During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam’s ϵ \epsilon and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron’s weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60 % 60\% to 99 % 99\% of the layer’s neurons at similar training and test accuracy. We vary which neurons share one equalization factor, from the whole layer to individual neurons, and find that the circuit stays concentrated for groups of eight or more and fully distributes only when every neuron has its own factor. Credit magnitudes are usually set by the built-in normalization of standard optimizers: Nero, which normalizes per neuron, distributes the computation, whereas Adam and seven others, including RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo, use other normalization schemes and retain small, concentrated circuits. Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion better, while concentrated circuits can be pruned further and transfer about twice as fast to a task that recombines the same features, largely by recruiting their unused neurons. Learning rule choice thus steers circuit size, trading robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the learned algorithm.

A neural network can reach nearly perfect training accuracy while test accuracy remains near zero for many epochs before improving abruptly. This delayed generalization is called grokking ( Power et al., 2022 ) . One can distinguish two aspects of a grokked solution: the computational procedure used to compute the function, which is called its algorithm , and how that procedure is implemented across neurons, which is called its circuit . Modular addition is a well-understood example of grokking and a central task in mechanistic interpretability of small networks. Its algorithm and circuit can both be analyzed at the neuron level: the network represents each operand as an angle on a circle at a few frequencies and adds the angles, a periodic computation carried by the neurons tuned to those frequencies ( Nanda et al., 2023 ; Gromov, 2023 ; Chughtai et al., 2023 ) . When we say that two networks learn the same algorithm, we mean that they share this Fourier-based computation (Appendix B.3 ).

The concentrated (i.e., small) circuits reported for modular addition leave open whether the concentration is required by the task or produced by the training procedure. Chughtai et al. (2023) describe the circuits learned for group composition in terms of group representations, but find that which representations a network learns, and in which order, varies across runs. Optimization research offers a potential explanation: the learning rule , i.e., the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, chooses among the many parameter settings that fit the training data ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ; Woodworth et al., 2020 ) . Yet the networks in these circuit studies have all been trained with similar learning rules based on backpropagation. In this paper, we ask how the learning rule selects the circuit that implements a learned algorithm: In our experiments on modular addition, the same periodic computation appears in circuits ranging from concentrated to nearly fully distributed. Effective circuit size varies across learning rules but little across random seeds. We investigate which property of the learning rule controls concentration and what the resulting differences imply for robustness and adaptability (Figure 1 ). Our object is the circuit of the grokked solution. Modular arithmetic provides a setting in which its algorithm is known, and the redistribution also appears on sparse parity, which generalizes without a delay (Appendix F.3 ).

Our central hypothesis is that circuit concentration depends on how the learning rule distributes credit across neurons, where credit denotes the learning signal assigned to a neuron. Backpropagation with Adam assigns unequal credit, and the neurons that receive little of it end with small outgoing weights (Figure 1 b). To isolate this effect, we modify backpropagation so that every neuron receives the same credit magnitude while its gradient direction is preserved, and we compare runs that share the data, initialization, loss, optimizer and hyperparameters. Equalizing credit increases the effective neuron count, computed from the outgoing weight norms, from approximately 154 154 to 254 254 of 256 256 neurons in the first hidden layer while retaining the periodic computation. Training loss remains the same within a few percent, and test accuracy is about two percentage points lower. Applied after grokking, the same intervention redistributes the outgoing weights of an already learned circuit at unchanged test accuracy. A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its update: the coupled weight decay in our reference, and Adam’s ϵ \epsilon or the decay of a normalization gain in other settings. This one condition accounts for three routes to unused neurons reported in separate lines of work ( Yaguchi et al., 2018 ; Mehta et al., 2019 ; Dufort-Labbé et al., 2025 ; Kolb et al., 2025 ) , and rebalancing each neuron undoes all three.

Both parts of the learning rule shape the credit: the credit assignment algorithm computes each neuron’s signal, and the optimizer rescales it. Rebalancing each neuron separately distributes the circuit, while groups of eight or more neurons that share one factor stay as concentrated as the reference. Among eight optimizers only Nero, which normalizes per neuron, produces a distributed circuit, and so does deep feedback control (DFC) ( Meulemans et al., 2021 ) , whose credit is nearly equal across neurons (Section 4.2 ).

Our contributions are the following. (i) Credit equalization, a controlled intervention on the learning rule that changes circuit concentration while the algorithm and the training fit stay the same and test accuracy stays within about two percentage points, including when applied after grokking. It shows that three routes to unused neurons, the coupled weight decay, Adam’s ϵ \epsilon and a decayed per-neuron gain, follow one per-neuron condition: the size of a neuron’s credit relative to the non-gradient term of its update. (ii) A controlled comparison shows that normalizing each neuron separately produces nearly uniform outgoing-weight participation, whereas normalizing larger groups retains concentration. (iii) A trade-off: distributed circuits better tolerate neuron deletion, whereas concentrated circuits can be pruned further and adapt about twice as fast from addition to subtraction, a task that recombines the learned operand frequencies, largely by recruiting their nearly unused neurons. The circuit that pruning extracts for the same algorithm changes several-fold with the training configuration. The redistribution holds on modular subtraction and multiplication, permutation composition in S 5 S_{5} , sparse parity and a transformer with a wide MLP, and changes little where the reference circuit is already distributed (Appendix F ).

Grokking was first reported on modular arithmetic and other small symbolic tasks ( Power et al., 2022 ) and later on image classification ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . Existing research explains the emergence of generalizing computations through circuit efficiency, that is, larger logits at a given parameter norm, which weight decay rewards ( Varma et al., 2023 ) , through the weight norm at initialization ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , and through a transition from nearly fixed initial features to learned task-specific features ( Kumar et al., 2024 ) . Nanda et al. (2023) track the Fourier circuit as it forms before test accuracy rises. A related theoretical analysis connects frequency selectivity with circuit size: after grokking, a one-hidden-layer network approaches solutions with single-frequency neurons and a computation distributed across many neurons ( Morwani et al., 2024 ) . Other studies report multiple solutions, but these differ in their algorithms rather than only in the number of units used. Changing the architecture, hyperparameters or seed can produce a different algorithm ( Zhong et al., 2023 ) . A sparse generalizing subnetwork can also coexist with a dense memorizing subnetwork ( Merrill et al., 2023 ) . Smaller initialization scales can concentrate a two-layer network into fewer effective neurons ( Luo et al., 2021 ) , without identifying which circuit will form. Closest to our finding, Manning-Coe et al. (2025) compare networks that grok with networks that generalize without delay and find that both learn the same features but encode them with different efficiency. Our comparison instead isolates credit allocation and measures how it distributes the circuit that implements the same algorithm.

The implicit-bias literature studies how optimization selects a solution among the many parameter settings that fit the training data. Such selection has been characterized for steepest descent under different norms ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ) and for product parameterizations with small initialization ( Woodworth et al., 2020 ) . On grokking tasks, parameterization scale affects feature learning ( Kumar et al., 2024 ) , and the optimizer affects whether grokking occurs ( Thilak et al., 2022 ) . With adaptive optimizers, an L2 penalty added to the gradient is rescaled together with it, so parameters with small gradients are regularized more strongly than under decoupled weight decay ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019 ) . We connect this selection to circuit concentration through a controlled intervention on credit allocation.

Adam with an L2 penalty drives whole nodes and filters to zero ( Yaguchi et al., 2018 ; Mehta et al., 2019 ) , Adam’s ϵ \epsilon lets units with tiny second-moment estimates die ( Dufort-Labbé et al., 2025 ) , decayed per-unit gains act as sparsity-inducing gates ( Mehta et al., 2019 ; Kolb et al., 2025 ) , and persistently small row-wise updates leave neurons dead under Muon in large language models ( Dewulf et al., 2026 ) . Under coupled L2 a neuron’s equilibrium depends on its gradient norm ( Kosson et al., 2024 ) . These works treat each route separately, as a pathology or a tool for pruning. We show that three of them share one per-neuron condition, that rebalancing each neuron controls all three, and that the condition decides how many neurons implement a fixed algorithm.

Several methods compute learning signals without using standard backpropagation. These include feedback alignment ( Lillicrap et al., 2016 ; Nøkland, 2016 ) , predictive coding ( Whittington & Bogacz, 2017 ) , equilibrium propagation ( Scellier & Bengio, 2017 ) , and deep feedback control (DFC) with its least control principle ( Meulemans et al., 2021 ; Meulemans et al., 2022 ) . They are usually evaluated by accuracy, which does not establish whether they learn the same computation or circuit as backpropagation. Refinetti et al. (2021) show that feedback alignment initially aligns with the gradient and later memorizes. Mallinar et al. (2025) demonstrate grokking without backpropagation in recursive feature machines, a kernel method without a neuron-level circuit.

We study modular arithmetic, a central task in grokking research (Section 2 ). The operands a , b ∈ ℤ p = { 0 , 1 , … , p − 1 } a,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}=\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\} are represented by concatenated one-hot vectors, and the target is c = ( a ∘ b ) mod p c=(a\circ b)\bmod p with ∘ ∈ { + , − , × } \circ\in\{+,-,\times\} . Our primary task is addition modulo the prime p = 31 p=31 . We use a fully connected ReLU network with two hidden layers of width 256 256 and a linear readout; multilayer perceptrons of this kind are standard in grokking studies of modular arithmetic ( Gromov, 2023 ; Morwani et al., 2024 ) . Unless stated otherwise, circuit measurements and neuron deletion concern the first hidden layer.

Our reference learning rule is backpropagation with Adam ( Kingma & Ba, 2015 ) , cross-entropy loss and coupled weight decay 10 − 3 10^{-3} , which adds the decay term to the gradient before Adam’s moment estimates (L2 regularization); Section 4.1 shows that this choice matters. Runs that we compare with each other share the data split and the initialization. We hold out 40 % 40\% of the operand pairs, train full batch, and apply credit equalization to the first hidden layer; budgets are stated with each experiment (Appendix A ). We classify a run as grokking when training accuracy reaches 1.0 1.0 and test accuracy first exceeds 0.95 0.95 at least 500 500 epochs later. Results are means over three seeds unless stated otherwise, with standard deviations in parentheses or as error bars.

We distinguish two parts of training. A credit assignment algorithm , such as backpropagation, computes a learning signal for each parameter. We call the signal received by a hidden neuron its credit . An optimizer , such as SGD or Adam, converts these signals into weight updates. We use learning rule for the combination of the two and vary each part in turn (Table 1 ). Credit equalization is the intervention we introduce. It rescales the magnitude of each neuron’s incoming-weight gradient before the gradient enters Adam and leaves its direction unchanged (Section 4.1 ). The optimizer comparison keeps backpropagation and replaces Adam with LARS, RMSProp, LAMB, Adafactor, Lion, Muon, Shampoo or Nero. DFC replaces the loss gradient by a controller-based signal. During training, a feedback controller drives the network output toward a target, its signal reaches each layer through the transposed Jacobian of the forward network, and each layer learns from the difference between its controlled and its feedforward activity ( Meulemans et al., 2021 ) . Section 4.3 asks which rules grok at all and adds six rules for that purpose. Feedback alignment and direct feedback alignment replace the transposed forward weights of the backward pass by fixed random matrices ( Lillicrap et al., 2016 ; Nøkland, 2016 ) , and sign-SGD keeps only the sign of each gradient coordinate ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ) . Three constructed rules add a component orthogonal to the gradient that is fresh at every step, fixed for the run, or fixed and fading with the training loss (Appendix H ). All six signals are passed to Adam, and the rules that memorize do not enter the circuit comparisons.

We ask how a learned computation is spread across the neurons of a layer in the networks that grok. On modular addition, algorithm checks for all the tested learning rules that grok show the same periodic Fourier computation and not the alternative computation reported by Zhong et al. (2023) (Appendix B.3 ). The checks cover the input frequencies used, a trigonometric fit of the logits, and agreement across seeds and rules; for the reference and the equalized network, the fitted trigonometric function alone classifies every held-out pair correctly. Two measures that use each neuron’s activity or its effect on the output also increase. Over eight seeds, participation computed from outgoing norms weighted by mean absolute activation rises from 0.34 0.34 to 0.81 0.81 . The activation-weighted measure is invariant to compensating rescalings of a ReLU neuron’s weights. We next ask whether the intervention can redistribute a circuit that has already been learned. We let the reference network grok, then switch to full credit equalization and continue training on the same task. Outgoing-weight participation rises from 0.60 0.60 to above 0.95 0.95 within 300 300 epochs and then to 0.99 0.99 , while test accuracy remains above 0.98 0.98 (Figure 2 b). The effect of the neurons on the output spreads as well, from ablation participation 0.40 0.40 to 0.72 0.72 over five seeds (Appendix E.4 ). A control that continues with the reference rule stays at 0.60 0.60 , and in separate runs both rules hold their participation over 200,000 200{,}000 epochs (Appendix C.4 ). Controls in Appendix C exclude alternative explanations. Constraining the incoming weight norms instead of the credit gives participation 0.66 0.66 , and a grid over learning rate and weight decay stays between 0.53 0.53 and 0.63 0.63 . Dropout also distributes the circuit, but it changes the objective and raises margin and norm (Appendix C.3 ). In a simplified linear model under gradient descent, each unit grows in proportion to its size without equalization and by the same amount with it, so initial differences persist in the first case and fade in the second (Proposition 3 , Appendix G ).

A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update. Adam is nearly invariant to a constant rescaling of its input, so rescaling a neuron’s gradient changes its size relative to the other terms of its update, in our reference the coupled decay term added to the gradient before Adam. Rescaling only this term per neuron, with the gradient unchanged, reproduces the redistribution, and equalizing the gradient while holding each neuron’s ratio of gradient to decay leaves the circuit concentrated, on the activation-weighted and ablation measures as well (Table 2 , Appendix C.6 ). The same condition holds for two other terms that do not scale with the gradient: Adam’s ϵ \epsilon , which dominates the denominator of its update when AdamW decays a transformer’s normalization parameters (Appendix F.5 ), and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain and of the outgoing weights (Appendix F.7 ). Lion and SGD with coupled decay follow it as well (Appendix C.3 ). Where no non-gradient term dominates, as under AdamW without decay on normalization parameters, the reference is already broadly distributed, with participation 0.91 0.91 . Full credit equalization is itself a normalization of the gradient with one factor per neuron. Optimizers normalize the learning signal at other scales: Adam normalizes each weight separately, LARS rescales a whole layer by one factor, and Nero normalizes the gradient of the weights into each neuron. Before comparing optimizers, we ask in a controlled setting whether normalizing several neurons together has the same effect as normalizing each one alone. For groups of eight or more neurons, circuit participation stays within about 0.02 0.02 of the value 0.60 0.60 of the reference, backpropagation with Adam. It rises to 0.70 0.70 for groups of four, 0.75 0.75 for pairs and 0.99 0.99 for single neurons (Figure 3 b). Most of the redistribution occurs only when each neuron receives its own factor. This equalizes the mean credit between groups but keeps the ratios inside a group: a neuron that received twice the credit of its neighbor still does after the rescaling. In a simplified model, a linear network in which every unit has one incoming and one outgoing scalar weight, these within-group differences persist throughout training and keep the circuit concentrated. Only single-neuron groups leave none to preserve (Proposition 4 in Appendix G , sweep details in Appendix D.1 ).

If per-neuron normalization is what distributes the circuit, optimizers should sort accordingly. We train with the eight optimizers of Table 1 that replace Adam. LARS, RMSProp, LAMB, Adafactor, Lion, Muon and Shampoo normalize groups other than a single neuron or change update directions, and all seven produce concentrated circuits, with participation between 0.470 0.470 and 0.613 0.613 . All seven run with the coupled weight decay of the reference. Nero, which uses no weight decay, produces at its default learning rate of 10 − 2 10^{-2} a distributed circuit with participation 0.986 0.986 at test accuracy 0.985 0.985 (Table 13 ). Nero, which normalizes credit per neuron, and DFC, whose credit is nearly equal (credit participation 0.94 0.94 ), are cases of equal credit that arise without our intervention, and both produce distributed circuits. For the reference, DFC and the equalization sweeps, credit participation lies close to circuit participation (Figure 3 a). The condition also explains why equal update norms do not suffice. Lion gives every neuron an update of the same norm, and Adam-mini ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) normalizes each neuron’s update with one second-moment estimate, yet both keep the circuit concentrated (Adam-mini 0.586 0.586 against 0.594 0.594 for Adam, Appendix D.1 ). Both normalize the coupled decay together with the gradient, so each neuron’s ratio of credit to decay is unchanged.

On modular addition, backpropagation with the optimizers in Table 1 , credit equalization, DFC and the two constructed rules with a fresh or a fading orthogonal component grok, whereas feedback alignment, direct feedback alignment, sign-SGD and the rule with a fixed orthogonal component fit the training set and stay near zero test accuracy over 15,000 15{,}000 epochs. This split matches the weight-decay account of grokking ( Nanda et al., 2023 ; Varma et al., 2023 ) . Once the training data are fitted, weight decay removes weight along the directions in which small parameter changes leave the training outputs unchanged, and a learning signal that is not a loss gradient can hold weight there. The norm q q of the weight in these directions (Appendix H ) separates the two outcomes at the end of training without overlap across nine configurations with three seeds each (Figure 1 a). It shrinks to means between 5.3 5.3 and 8.5 8.5 in the rules that grok and stays between 26 26 and 135 135 in the rules that memorize. Within a rule, q q does not predict the outcome (Appendix H ).

chunks.section: 5 Relevance: Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion, concentrated circuits keep spare capacity
chunks.text: Throughout this section the concentrated circuit is the reference ( β = 0 \beta=0 ) and the distributed circuit is the fully equalized network ( β = 1 \beta=1 ), both trained on modular addition at p = 31 p=31 .

A computation spread over many neurons should depend less on any single one of them ( Georgopoulos et al., 1986 ) , and networks that generalize well are known to rely less on single units ( Morcos et al., 2018 ) . In an additive model, the relative fluctuation of the output under random deletion falls with the effective neuron count (Proposition 5 , Appendix G ). We test this with three deletion procedures, all applied to the first hidden layer of the trained network without retraining. Random deletion removes a random subset of the neurons. Norm-ranked deletion removes neurons in decreasing order of outgoing norm, so the neurons a concentrated circuit relies on go first. Greedy deletion removes, at each step, the neuron whose removal lowers test accuracy the most. For random and norm-ranked deletion we report the neuron-deletion tolerance , or deletion tolerance for short, the normalized area under the curve of test accuracy against the deleted fraction from 0 0 to 0.8 0.8 . For greedy deletion we report the number of neurons removed before test accuracy falls below 0.5 0.5 (Appendix E.1 ). We take networks that have grokked addition at each β \beta and fine-tune the whole network on a new operation with backpropagation with Adam. The adaptation time is the number of fine-tuning epochs until test accuracy on the new operation reaches 0.9 0.9 . We compare it with training a new network from scratch. We first transfer to subtraction, which uses the same Fourier frequencies as addition and differs in how they are combined. Training from scratch takes 1410 1410 epochs. Starting from the concentrated addition circuit takes 640 640 epochs, so the pretrained circuit helps. Starting from the distributed circuit takes 1540 1540 epochs, no faster than from scratch, and the adaptation time increases monotonically with β \beta in between (Appendix E.4 ). The concentrated circuit adapts about 2.4 2.4 times as fast as the distributed one. The ordering holds at one third and at three times the fine-tuning learning rate, in the reverse transfer from subtraction to addition, when an outgoing-norm constraint sets the participation of the source network, and when both networks are fine-tuned with credit equalization instead of the reference rule (Appendices E.3 and E.4 ). The difference also appears when both continue from the same grokked checkpoint, with 1052 1052 against 608 608 epochs, slower in all five seed pairs.

Much of the advantage comes from the nearly unused neurons. With them removed from the concentrated network at unchanged test accuracy, adaptation to subtraction takes 1204 1204 instead of 652 652 epochs, against 1480 1480 for the distributed network, so they account for about two thirds of the difference. On ( b − a ) mod p (b-a)\bmod p they account for about half (five seeds, Appendix E.4 ). Networks distributed by per-neuron decay alone adapt as slowly as equalized ones, so across the tested interventions adaptation follows the circuit, not the rule that produced it. Targets that keep the hidden features of addition and change only the readout, ( a + b + 7 ) mod p (a+b+7)\bmod p and a fixed permutation of ( a + b ) mod p (a+b)\bmod p , are learned 2.3 2.3 to 6.6 6.6 times faster than from scratch, with no consistent advantage for either circuit. We repeat the experiment with multiplication, which does not share the Fourier frequency representation of addition. Every pretrained network takes 1800 1800 to 2020 2020 epochs, compared with 1200 1200 from scratch, so pretraining on addition does not help at any β \beta .

Circuit concentration is a consequence of the training dynamics and not of the task alone. The concentrated circuits found under backpropagation with Adam are one of several ways a grokked solution can be implemented. A neuron stops contributing when its credit is small relative to the non-gradient term of its update, whether that term is the coupled decay, Adam’s ϵ \epsilon or the decay of a gain, and learning rules that rebalance each neuron keep it in use. The condition also governs MLP units in a 30 30 M-parameter language model trained with Adam and L2 regularization, where balancing each unit’s decay leaves 1.3 % 1.3\% instead of 24 % 24\% nearly unused at lower validation loss, and AdamW leaves 0.9 % 0.9\% , as the condition predicts (Appendix F.8 ). For mechanistic interpretability this means that the size of a circuit found in a trained network, including the circuit that pruning extracts, reflects the learning rule and how weight decay enters it, as well as the task. A sparse circuit read out of a network trained with Adam is a property of that training run, and comparing learning rules separates what the task requires from what the optimizer selected. A distributed circuit loses less when units are removed, as under a hardware fault, while pruning and fine-tuning profit from the nearly unused neurons of a concentrated circuit, which can be removed at no cost or recruited by a related task that needs new hidden features. On modular addition, the choice of learning rule trades robustness to neuron loss against compressibility and spare capacity, without changing the learned algorithm.

The theory isolates the distribution mechanism in a simplified linear model without adaptive normalization and covers rescalings that preserve update directions. The results on nonlinear networks and on optimizers are empirical. Under AdamW without decay on normalization parameters the remaining effect is small (participation 0.91 0.91 to 0.96 0.96 ) and not explained by the condition, and for Adam’s ϵ \epsilon holding the per-neuron ratio fixed removes about half of the effect. The algorithm checks cover modular addition only. The adaptation advantage appears for targets that need new hidden combinations of the operand frequencies and not for targets that change only the readout. The robustness advantage concerns the deletion of neurons.

chunks.section: B.1 Do outgoing norms reflect the distribution of computation?
chunks.text: We use the participation ratio of outgoing norms rather than a Fourier-based sparsity measure because it needs no Fourier basis, applies unchanged to every task we study, and is invariant to a uniform rescaling of the outgoing weights. It is, however, a structural measure. The network’s function is unchanged when a ReLU neuron’s incoming weights and bias are multiplied by a positive constant and its outgoing weights are divided by the same constant, so outgoing norms could in principle change without any change in the computation. We check the redistribution with two measures that are tied to the computation.

chunks.section: Appendix C Controls on credit equalization
chunks.text: The main experiment changes the credit magnitudes and observes a change in the outgoing weights. This section tests the alternative explanations: that the effect comes from the incoming weight norms rather than from the credit, that it depends on which neurons receive the credit, that Adam or the hyperparameters produce it, and that the concentrated circuit is only a transient state.

Full credit equalization gives every neuron the same gradient norm, and Nero, which also distributes the circuit, additionally constrains the weight norms. Could equal incoming weight norms alone explain the redistribution? We test two constraints on the weights that leave the gradients unchanged. The first renormalizes each neuron’s incoming weights to a fixed norm after every update. Circuit participation is 0.661 ​ ( 0.015 ) 0.661\,(0.015) , compared with 0.595 ​ ( 0.023 ) 0.595\,(0.023) for the reference, and deletion tolerance decreases (Table 8 , upper block). The second is weight normalization ( Salimans & Kingma, 2016 ) , which parameterizes each incoming weight vector as a direction times a learned scale; with weight decay on the scales it groks to test accuracy 0.993 0.993 with participation 0.466 ​ ( 0.026 ) 0.466\,(0.026) . Neither constraint approaches the participation of 0.99 0.99 reached by credit equalization. Equal incoming weight norms do not reproduce the redistribution.

chunks.section: C.2 Assigning credit independently of neuron identity
chunks.text: In the first hidden layer, a neuron’s incoming-weight gradient is the input multiplied by the backpropagated error, and that error depends linearly on the neuron’s outgoing weights. Credit and outgoing norms are therefore coupled at every step, and their agreement could reflect this coupling rather than an effect of the credit on the circuit. We break the coupling by assigning credit magnitudes that carry no information about the neurons. A credit profile is a vector of n n nonnegative target magnitudes with a chosen participation ratio. At every step we replace the incoming-gradient norms by this profile, scaled so that the total norm is preserved, and keep every gradient’s direction. A random permutation, drawn once per run, decides which neuron receives which magnitude, so the assignment is independent of the neurons’ roles. Circuit participation follows the imposed value, from 0.637 0.637 at profile participation 0.60 0.60 to 0.990 0.990 at 1.00 1.00 , deletion tolerance increases with it, and test accuracy stays above 0.96 0.96 (Table 8 , lower block). An allocation chosen independently of the neurons’ current roles therefore sets the final concentration.

chunks.section: C.2 Assigning credit independently of neuron identity
chunks.text: A second control keeps the reference’s credit magnitudes at each step but randomly reassigns them to the neurons at every step. Each permutation preserves that step’s participation and changes only which neurons receive the largest signals. Final circuit participation is 0.992 0.992 , compared with 0.613 0.613 for the reference. Measured over the last 800 800 epochs, credit participation is 0.979 0.979 rather than the reference’s 0.604 0.604 : once the assignment no longer favors the same neurons, the trained network itself develops more uniform gradients. This suggests that concentration requires the credit to stay concentrated on the same neurons over time. The effect persists across the tested initialization scales. Across scales from 0.5 0.5 to 4 4 , reference participation is 0.586 0.586 to 0.613 0.613 and full equalization gives 0.990 0.990 to 0.998 0.998 , with a mean absolute difference of 0.008 0.008 between credit and circuit participation. chunks.section: C.6 Gradient and weight decay under Adam
chunks.text: Our reference adds the coupled decay term λ ​ 𝒘 j \lambda{\bm{w}}_{j} to each neuron’s incoming-weight gradient 𝒈 j {\bm{g}}_{j} before Adam, whose update is nearly invariant to a constant rescaling of its input. Full credit equalization multiplies 𝒈 j {\bm{g}}_{j} by s j = g ¯ / ‖ 𝒈 j ‖ 2 s_{j}=\bar{g}/\|{\bm{g}}_{j}\|_{2} and leaves the decay term unchanged, so it also changes the ratio between the two. We separate the two effects with four conditions that differ only in how each first-layer neuron’s gradient and decay term are scaled before Adam, with s j s_{j} recomputed at every step (Table 12 ). The decay is added after clipping, where Adam adds coupled decay, and biases and the other layers keep the decay λ \lambda . Scaling only the decay term, by 1 / s j 1/s_{j} , gives the participation of full equalization, 0.993 0.993 , no nearly unused neurons and nearly the same deletion tolerance, and it is more distributed still on the activation-weighted and ablation measures ( 0.981 0.981 and 0.924 0.924 against 0.850 0.850 and 0.832 0.832 ). Scaling both the gradient and the decay term by s j s_{j} keeps each neuron’s ratio of gradient to decay as in the reference and gives the reference circuit, with participation 0.574 0.574 and 92 92 nearly unused neurons. Under Adam with coupled weight decay, the intervention therefore acts through this ratio. Adam’s invariance holds exactly only for a constant factor, and s j s_{j} changes from step to step, so the two conditions do not give identical updates; the controls measure their effect on the circuit directly.

chunks.text: Section 4.2 shows that the number of neurons sharing one normalization factor decides how far the circuit is redistributed. This section gives the details of that sweep. We divide the 256 256 neurons of the first hidden layer into g g equal groups of m = n / g m=n/g neurons, fixed at the start of the run, and at every step multiply all gradients in a group by the common factor of Equation 3 , so that the mean credit is equal across groups while the relative magnitudes within a group are unchanged; a group whose gradients are all zero is left unchanged. Group size m = 256 m=256 corresponds to no rescaling and reproduces the reference: 0.602 ​ ( 0.023 ) 0.602\,(0.023) against 0.60 ​ ( 0.02 ) 0.60\,(0.02) in the β \beta sweep. Group size m = 1 m=1 rescales each neuron separately and reproduces full credit equalization: 0.992 0.992 against 0.99 0.99 at β = 1 \beta=1 . Across the per-neuron settings, credit and circuit participation differ by 0.0074 0.0074 on average within seeds, which is the vertical distance from the identity line in Figure 3 a. Most of the change happens at the smallest groups. Going from pairs to single neurons raises circuit participation from 0.753 0.753 to 0.992 0.992 , about 61 % 61\% of the total increase from the whole-layer value, and norm-ranked deletion tolerance from 0.327 0.327 to 0.576 0.576 . Groups of four and two give intermediate values. Per-neuron rescaling of the credit is thus the setting most likely to distribute a circuit, and coarser groups keep most of the concentration. On S 5 S_{5} the sweep gives 0.749 0.749 for groups of four, 0.852 0.852 for pairs and 0.974 0.974 for single neurons, the same pattern as on modular addition.

Adam-mini ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) uses one second-moment estimate per row of each weight matrix, that is, per output neuron. With coupled decay it normalizes each neuron’s gradient and decay term together, so their ratio stays as in Adam. On modular addition with the reference settings and five fresh seeds, its circuit participation is 0.586 0.586 against 0.594 0.594 for Adam, and greedy pruning keeps 72 72 neurons against 70 70 at test accuracy 0.95 0.95 (Appendix E.2 ). Per-neuron normalization distributes the circuit only when it changes each neuron’s credit relative to its decay.

The controlled sweep varies only the group size and preserves the direction of every neuron’s gradient before Adam. Optimizers combine a group structure with other transformations, so we ask whether they nevertheless sort by their normalization group. Table 13 reports test accuracy, credit participation and circuit participation for the eight optimizers of Table 1 with the settings of Appendix A . LARS (one factor per layer), RMSProp and Lion (per parameter), LAMB (per parameter with a layerwise trust ratio), Adafactor (factored per-parameter scaling), and Muon and Shampoo (matrix transformations) all produce concentrated circuits, with participation between 0.470 0.470 and 0.613 0.613 , although their credit participation ranges from 0.478 0.478 to 1.000 1.000 . Nero normalizes per neuron and produces a distributed circuit. At its default learning rate 10 − 2 10^{-2} and at 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , it generalizes with test accuracy 0.985 0.985 and 0.978 0.978 and participation 0.986 ​ ( 0.002 ) 0.986\,(0.002) and 0.983 ​ ( 0.001 ) 0.983\,(0.001) (lower block of Table 13 ). It also tolerates neuron deletion better than the reference: random-deletion tolerance is 0.748 0.748 and norm-ranked tolerance 0.626 0.626 ( 0.728 0.728 and 0.541 0.541 at the smaller learning rate), against 0.672 0.672 and 0.311 0.311 for the reference in the same experiment, close to the values of the equalized network. A per-neuron optimizer thus provides the same robustness as our intervention. Because Nero holds each neuron’s incoming-weight norm fixed, its outgoing-norm participation cannot arise from scale moving between a neuron’s incoming and outgoing weights, the rescaling symmetry discussed in Appendix B.1 .

Proposition 4 covers positive rescalings that preserve update directions, whereas per-parameter and matrix transformations rotate the update, so the optimizer comparison extends the controlled sweep empirically. NorMuon ( Li et al., 2025 ) adds a per-neuron normalization after Muon’s orthogonalization, motivated by the unequal neuron update norms that Muon produces, the same inequality that concentrates the circuit here. Deleting a first-hidden-layer neuron sets its outgoing weights to zero; the network is then evaluated on the test set without retraining. Random deletion removes fractions 0 , 0.1 , … , 0.8 0,0.1,\ldots,0.8 of the layer, with 20 20 random masks per fraction ( 30 30 in the ten-seed experiment of Figure 1 c). Deletion tolerance is the area under the curve of test accuracy against the deleted fraction at these nine fractions, computed by the trapezoidal rule and divided by the range 0.8 0.8 , so that it lies between 0 0 and 1 1 . Norm-ranked deletion removes neurons in decreasing order of outgoing norm at the same fractions. Greedy deletion evaluates every remaining neuron, removes the one whose removal lowers test accuracy the most, and repeats until accuracy falls below 0.5 0.5 ; we report the number of neurons removed. Greedy deletion selects neurons by their effect on the test set rather than by their weights. Table 15 compares the reference, full credit equalization and DFC under random and norm-ranked deletion in one matched three-seed experiment (Figure 6 ). Equalization improves tolerance under both procedures, and the improvement is larger under norm-ranked deletion, which removes exactly the neurons a concentrated circuit relies on. DFC lies between the two. Table 16 reports greedy deletion for the reference and three equalization strengths: the number of neurons that must be removed grows with participation, from 23 23 at β = 0 \beta=0 to 61 61 at β = 1 \beta=1 . The deletion advantage of the distributed circuit thus does not depend on selecting neurons by their norm. Over ten seeds, random-deletion tolerance is 0.672 ​ ( 0.012 ) 0.672\,(0.012) for the reference and 0.773 ​ ( 0.014 ) 0.773\,(0.014) under full equalization (Figure 1 c).

We remove first-hidden-layer neurons in increasing order of outgoing norm (magnitude pruning) and, greedily, the neuron whose removal raises the training cross-entropy least, and record test accuracy without retraining (Table 14 ; five seeds, the networks of Table 12 ). The concentrated circuit keeps test accuracy above 0.9 0.9 until 62 % 62\% of its neurons are removed by magnitude, against 20 % 20\% for the distributed circuit. Greedy removal takes away 191 191 against 160 160 neurons before test accuracy falls below 0.9 0.9 , and 177 177 against 117 117 before it falls below 0.95 0.95 . The nearly unused neurons of the concentrated circuit can be removed at no cost, so it is the easier circuit to compress. chunks.section: E.3 Matching participation through outgoing-weight constraints
chunks.text: Does the deletion advantage depend on how the distributed circuit was trained, or only on the resulting distribution of outgoing norms? We compare two ways of reaching the same circuit participation. Credit equalization changes the gradients. An outgoing-norm constraint leaves the gradients unchanged and instead rescales the outgoing weights of the first hidden layer after every update to a prescribed norm profile with participation 0.60 0.60 , 0.80 0.80 or 0.99 0.99 ; the profile has two norm levels, each shared by half of the neurons. All conditions use five seeds (Table 19 ).

At participation 0.99 0.99 , credit equalization and the outgoing-norm constraint give the same random-deletion tolerance, 0.777 0.777 ; at participation 0.60 0.60 , the constrained network and the reference differ by 0.02 0.02 . Greedy deletion removes 66.7 ​ ( 11.1 ) 66.7\,(11.1) neurons under equalization and 68.7 ​ ( 10.8 ) 68.7\,(10.8) under the constraint before accuracy falls below 0.5 0.5 . Deletion tolerance thus follows the distribution of outgoing norms in both ways of producing it.

We also fine-tune these networks from addition to subtraction and measure the epochs to test accuracy 0.9 0.9 , evaluated every 20 20 epochs. Within the constrained networks, adaptation takes 740 740 , 1228 1228 and 1480 1480 epochs at participation 0.60 0.60 , 0.80 0.80 and 0.99 0.99 ; the equalized network takes 1608 1608 epochs. Adaptation slows with participation under both interventions. At participation 0.60 0.60 , the reference takes 464 464 epochs and the constrained network 740 740 : the reference has 87 87 neurons with an outgoing norm below one tenth of the layer mean, which the new task can recruit, whereas the constraint holds every neuron at one of two norms and leaves none. The difference points to the low-norm neurons, which a related task can recruit. chunks.section: E.4 Adaptation to a new operation
chunks.text: Networks first grok addition at p = 31 p=31 at each β \beta . We then fine-tune the whole network on the new operation with the reference rule, backpropagation with Adam at learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} and a fresh optimizer state, in every condition, on the new operation’s own split with 40 % 40\% of the pairs held out, and record the number of epochs until test accuracy on the new operation reaches 0.9 0.9 , evaluated every 100 100 epochs (Table 22 ).

Adaptation time increases with the participation of the source circuit at every step, from 640 640 epochs at β = 0 \beta=0 to 1540 1540 at β = 1 \beta=1 ; training from scratch takes 1410 1410 epochs. The seed ranges at the two endpoints do not overlap: 400 400 to 800 800 epochs at β = 0 \beta=0 against 1200 1200 to 1800 1800 at β = 1 \beta=1 . An independent ten-seed run, evaluated every 20 20 epochs, gives 690 ​ ( 164 ) 690\,(164) and 1550 ​ ( 191 ) 1550\,(191) epochs. Pretraining on addition helps from the concentrated circuit and not from the distributed one.

We count the neurons whose outgoing norm is below one tenth of the layer mean. The reference has about 85 85 such neurons. Our hypothesis is that subtraction can recruit them with little disturbance to the addition circuit. Already at β = 0.25 \beta=0.25 the count is zero, and adaptation time rises from 640 640 to 940 940 epochs. It keeps rising to 1540 1540 epochs at β = 1 \beta=1 as the circuit spreads further, which is consistent with the new operation having to modify a larger share of a distributed representation. In continual learning, inactive units signal a loss of plasticity that resetting them restores ( Sokar et al., 2023 ; Dohare et al., 2024 ) ; here the low-norm neurons of the reference circuit coincide with faster adaptation, which suggests that unused capacity can serve a related task when the rest of the circuit stays intact.

We test credit equalization on sparse parity, a task used to study how networks find a few relevant features after a long plateau ( Barak et al., 2022 ) . The input is a vector of 20 20 bits, each 0 0 or 1 1 ; the label is 1 1 if an odd number of three fixed bits are set and 0 0 otherwise, so the remaining 17 17 bits are distractors that the network has to ignore. We draw 4000 4000 or 600 600 inputs at random from the 2 20 2^{20} possibilities and assign each to the training or the test set with probability one half, which gives about 2000 2000 and 300 300 training examples. The runs generalize without delay under full-batch training, so this experiment tests the redistribution outside the grokking regime. Equalization raises circuit participation from 0.15 0.15 to 0.96 0.96 on the larger dataset and from 0.08 0.08 to 0.89 0.89 on the smaller one. Test accuracy is 1.000 1.000 for both conditions on the larger dataset and changes from 1.000 1.000 to 0.988 0.988 on the smaller one, and random-deletion tolerance improves at both sizes (Table 27 ).
